\chapter{Le — Finished, and Changed}
\label{ch:zh-le}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that an action is finished, that a situation has changed, and explain why neither of those is a tense.}

Two strokes — fewer than any character in the book but \zh{一} and \zh{二} — and with them the first sentences in this track that are not happening now.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[le]{\zh{了} — two strokes}

\label{lesson:ZH-W25-le}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and the smallest character in it does the most.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ yǒu yí ge míngzi} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shí} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shí} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{guó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sheng} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — a turn, and a hook}
\begin{quote}
\zh{了}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two strokes.} Only \zh{一} and \zh{二} have used fewer.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héngpiě}: start with a short flat run at the upper left, then let it fall away to the right — \textbf{one stroke, one turn, no lift}
  \item the \textbf{shùgōu}: lift, come down from under that turn almost to the floor of the square, and flick left at the very end
\end{enumerate}

The hook at the foot is not decoration; it is what tells \zh{了} apart from a bare vertical. Finish it.

You have written a \textbf{héngzhé} — a horizontal that turns down — in every \zh{口} since the fourth chapter. This is its cousin: the turn does not go straight down, it falls away.

\textbf{Two strokes, and no tone.} For a character that carries more grammar than any other in this book, it asks remarkably little of the hand.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{了} — the turn, then the hooked vertical
  \item \emph{Cover:} write it again, and check the hook is there
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{了} have? (\textbf{Two}.) Which characters use fewer? (\textbf{\zh{一} and \zh{二}}.) What must the second stroke end with? (\textbf{A hook to the left}.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E4\%BA\%86.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{了}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le]{\zh{我看了书} — the thing is done}

\label{lesson:ZH-C25-le-dongci}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the character is already under your pen.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yī èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā jiǔ shí} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shíyī} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xuésheng} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: verb + \zh{了} = finished}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{了}} \emph{le} — toneless, and placed \textbf{straight after the verb}. It says the action is \textbf{complete}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我看书}} — I read. / I'm reading. \textbf{\zh{我看了书}} \emph{wǒ kàn le shū} — I read it. I've read it. Done.
\end{quote}

The verb did not move and did not change — the last chapter's rule holds. One small word went in behind it, and the event closed.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我有了名字}} — I've got a name now. \textbf{\zh{你看了吗}} \emph{nǐ kàn le ma} — have you read it?
\end{quote}

That last one puts \zh{了} and \zh{吗} in the same sentence, each doing its own job at its own end: \zh{了} sits behind the verb, \zh{吗} at the very finish.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the past this book could not reach}]
Until this line, \textbf{everything in this book happened in an eternal present.} Every sentence you could build was now, and there was no way to say a thing had already happened.

Spanish spends an imperfect, a preterite with two irregular sets, a present perfect and two participles on the same job. English has \emph{read}, \emph{have read}, \emph{had read}, \emph{was reading}. Mandarin has \textbf{\zh{了}} and, when it needs one, a word for \emph{yesterday}.

The verb still does not change. It never will. What changed is that a finished event can now be told apart from an unfinished one — and that is done by adding a particle, not by reshaping a word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我看书} — \zh{我看了书}
  \item \emph{wǒ yǒu le míngzi} — \zh{我有了名字}
  \item \zh{你看了吗}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \zh{了} go? (\textbf{Straight after the verb}.) What does it say? (\textbf{The action is finished}.) What happened to the verb when you added it? (\textbf{Nothing} — verbs never change.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǒ shì dàxuéshēng le]{\zh{我是大学生了} — something has changed}

\label{lesson:ZH-C25-le-juwei}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and the same character in a different slot.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{èrshí} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bǎi} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xué} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \zh{了} at the end says the situation is new}]
Put \zh{了} at the very \textbf{end} of a sentence, after everything else, and it stops talking about the verb and starts talking about the situation:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是大学生了}} \emph{wǒ shì dàxuéshēng le} — I'm a university student \textbf{now}. \textbf{\zh{有人了}} — somebody's here \textbf{now}. \textbf{\zh{我看书了}} — I'm reading now. \emph{(I wasn't before)}
\end{quote}

This \zh{了} hangs off a whole finished sentence, not off any one word in it. That is why it goes last and why nothing may follow it.

\textbf{The English word that keeps appearing in those translations is \emph{now}, and it is not a translation of \zh{了}.} It is what English has to reach for to carry what \zh{了} does: \emph{this was not so before, and it is so now.} Nothing in the Mandarin says \emph{now}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是大学生}} — I am a university student. \emph{(a fact)} \textbf{\zh{我是大学生了}} — I've become one. \emph{(a change)}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two slots, two jobs, one character.} Behind the verb, \zh{了} closes an action. At the end of the sentence, it opens a new state. This is what a language does when it refuses to inflect: it moves a small word around instead of reshaping a big one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我是大学生} — \zh{我是大学生了}
  \item \zh{有人了}
  \item \zh{我看了书} — \zh{我看书了}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does this \zh{了} go? (\textbf{At the very end of the sentence}.) What does it say? (\textbf{Something has changed}.) Is it the same character as the last lesson's? (\textbf{Yes} — same two strokes, different slot, different job.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le]{\zh{了} — aspect, and why it is not a tense}

\label{lesson:ZH-C25-ti}



\begin{quote}
The chapter's fourth lesson, and it names what the other three were doing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shì dàxuéshēng le} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yìbǎi} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǔ} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xué} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Mandarin marks completion, not time}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{了} is not a past tense.} It marks \textbf{aspect} — whether an event is complete — and says nothing at all about when it happened.
\end{quote}

Here is the proof, and it is the reason this lesson exists:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我看了书}} — I read the book. \emph{(finished — could be an hour ago)} \textbf{\zh{我看了书你看吗}} — I've finished the book; are you going to read it?
\end{quote}

The second sentence is not in the past. \zh{了} says the reading is \textbf{over}, and whether that was this morning or will be by tonight is settled by a time word, not by the verb and not by \zh{了}.

\textbf{So Mandarin splits the job English and Spanish fuse.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{when} it happened & a time word — \emph{yesterday}, \emph{now}, \emph{tomorrow} \\
\textbf{whether} it is finished & a particle — \zh{了} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An English verb carries both at once: \emph{read} against \emph{reads} against \emph{have read}. A Spanish verb carries both and the person as well. Mandarin carries neither in the verb, because the verb does not change — the last chapter's rule, arriving where it matters most.

\textbf{This is the single largest shape difference between Mandarin and the languages this book's reader is likeliest to arrive from}, and \zh{了} is where a beginner first meets it. \zh{了} is one of several aspect particles; the others come later.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{我看了书}
  \item \zh{我看了书你看吗}
  \item aspect is \emph{whether it is finished}; tense is \emph{when}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \zh{了} a past tense? (\textbf{No} — it is aspect.) What does it actually mark? (\textbf{Whether the event is finished}.) What settles when something happened? (\textbf{A time word}, not the verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{我看了书}}

\label{lesson:ZH-C25-practice}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes on two strokes.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{le} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ yǒu yí ge míngzi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shíyī èrshí jiúshíjiǔ yìbǎi} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎo bu hǎo} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì — hànzì — hànyǔ — zhōngwén — zhōngguó} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dàjiā} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — two strokes, and time itself}]
Before this chapter every sentence in this book happened now. After it:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{我看了书}} — a finished action. \zh{了} behind the verb.
  \item \textbf{\zh{我是大学生了}} — a changed state. \zh{了} at the end.
  \item \textbf{Neither is a tense.} Mandarin marks whether, not when.
\end{enumerate}

Two strokes did that. Compare the price: the verb chapter needed a character each for \zh{看} and \zh{书}, and neither of them changed what could be \emph{said about time}.

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Wǒ kàn le shū. Wǒ shì dàxuéshēng le. Nǐ kàn le ma?}

\textbf{Speak.} Say you have read the book; then say you have become a student.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{我看了书} — \zh{有人了} — \zh{你看了吗}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{了} — the turn, then the hook.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我看了书}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我是大学生了}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{你看了吗}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{了}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the two slots \zh{了} uses and what each does. (\textbf{After the verb, the action is finished; at the end, the situation has changed}.) Is either one a tense? (\textbf{No} — both are aspect.) How many strokes? (\textbf{Two}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
